circulus-arteriosus.summary: Ring of arteries at the base of the brain, around the pituitary stalk and the optic chiasm, that links the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems.
facts: Internal carotid arteries and basilar artery
Forms a ring around the interpeduncular fossa
Anterior cerebral artery (both sides), anterior communicating artery, internal carotid artery (terminal part), posterior communicating artery (both sides), posterior cerebral artery (both sides)

Anterior cerebral artery: medial surface of the hemispheres (motor and sensory area of the leg); middle cerebral artery: lateral surface (face and arm, language areas); posterior cerebral artery: occipital lobe and inferior surface of the temporal lobe, thalamus
clinical: Most brain aneurysms (berry aneurysms) develop in the front of the ring, especially at the anterior communicating artery; their rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Variations of the ring are common; only 20–25% of people have a 'classic' complete ring.
tus: Variations of the circle of Willis are frequent; a complete circle is found in only about half of people.
A PCom aneurysm may present with oculomotor nerve palsy, an ACom aneurysm with a visual field defect and SAH.

a-subclavia.summary: The main artery of the upper limb, which also gives important branches to the neck and chest wall. At the outer border of the first rib it becomes the axillary artery.
facts: On the right the brachiocephalic trunk, on the left the aortic arch
Passes in front of the cervical pleura, behind the anterior scalene (scalene gap) and over the 1st rib towards the arm
Vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery, thyrocervical trunk, costocervical trunk, dorsal scapular artery
Upper limb, brain (vertebral artery), neck, anterior chest wall and breast (internal thoracic artery)
clinical: Subclavian steal syndrome: narrowing of the subclavian artery before the origin of the vertebral artery causes dizziness when the arm is exercised.
The artery can be punctured by mistake while a central venous catheter is placed.
tus: The subclavian artery is divided into three parts by the anterior scalene; the vertebral, internal thoracic and thyrocervical trunk arise from the 1st part.
A right subclavian artery arising as the last branch of the aortic arch (arteria lusoria) can compress the oesophagus and cause difficulty swallowing (dysphagia lusoria).

a-axillaris.summary: Continuation of the subclavian artery from the outer border of the first rib to the lower border of teres major. Pectoralis minor divides it into three parts.
facts: Continuation of the subclavian artery (outer border of the 1st rib)
Descends through the axilla surrounded by the cords of the brachial plexus; at the lower border of teres major it becomes the brachial artery
1st part: superior thoracic artery; 2nd part: thoraco-acromial artery, lateral thoracic artery; 3rd part: subscapular artery, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries
Shoulder, chest wall, mammary gland, axilla
clinical: It can be injured in shoulder dislocations and fractures of the neck of the humerus.
A rich collateral network around the scapula (scapular anastomosis) supplies the arm when the subclavian artery is blocked.
tus: The axillary artery starts at the outer border of the 1st rib and becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major.
The axillary artery can be injured in shoulder dislocations and fractures of the neck of the humerus.

a-brachialis.summary: The main artery of the arm; it descends on the inner side of the arm along the medial border of biceps and divides at the elbow into the radial and ulnar arteries.
facts: Continuation of the axillary artery (lower border of teres major)
Descends on the inner side of the arm with the median nerve; in the cubital fossa, under the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides at the level of the neck of the radius
Profunda brachii artery (with the radial nerve), superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries, muscular branches; terminal branches the radial and ulnar arteries
Muscles of the arm, humerus, region of the elbow joint
clinical: When blood pressure is measured, the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa.
It can be injured in supracondylar fractures of the humerus in children; ischaemia of the forearm leads to Volkmann's contracture.
tus: The brachial artery runs on the inner side of the arm with the median nerve; the nerve crosses the artery from lateral to medial at mid-arm.
It divides into the radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa (level of the neck of the radius).

a-radialis.summary: Artery running on the outer (thumb) side of the forearm; it is the artery most often used to take the pulse.
facts: Brachial artery (cubital fossa)

Descends on the lateral side of the forearm under brachioradialis; at the wrist it is superficial, lateral to the FCR tendon, then passes through the anatomical snuffbox to the back of the hand and enters the palm through the 1st interosseous space to form the deep palmar arch
Radial recurrent artery, superficial palmar branch, palmar and dorsal carpal branches, princeps pollicis artery, radialis indicis artery
Lateral forearm, wrist, thumb and index finger, deep structures of the hand
clinical: The radial pulse is taken at the wrist; it is the artery most often used for arterial blood gases.
Before cannulation, the Allen test checks whether the ulnar artery alone can supply the hand.
Coronary angiography is increasingly performed through the radial artery.
tus: The radial artery crosses the floor of the snuffbox and enters the palm between the two heads of the 1st dorsal interosseous to form the deep arch.
The radial artery is used as a graft in coronary bypass and as an access route for cardiac catheterisation.

a-ulnaris.summary: The larger of the two terminal branches of the brachial artery, running on the inner (little finger) side of the forearm.
facts: Brachial artery (cubital fossa)
Descends on the deep forearm flexors under FCU; at the wrist it passes through Guyon's canal with the ulnar nerve and forms the superficial palmar arch
Ulnar recurrent arteries, common interosseous artery (anterior and posterior interosseous arteries), palmar and dorsal carpal branches, deep palmar branch
Medial and deep parts of the forearm (through the interosseous arteries), most of the hand
tus: At the wrist the ulnar artery lies lateral to the FCU tendon and lateral to the ulnar nerve.

arcus-palmares.summary: Two anastomotic arterial arches in the palm formed by the radial and ulnar arteries; the branches to the fingers arise from them.
facts: Superficial arch: mainly the ulnar artery; deep arch: mainly the radial artery
Superficial arch under the palmar aponeurosis, deep arch under the flexor tendons at the level of the bases of the metacarpals
Common and proper palmar digital arteries (superficial); palmar metacarpal arteries (deep)
Palm and fingers
clinical: The superficial arch is easily injured in cuts of the palm and causes serious bleeding.
tus: The superficial palmar arch lies more distally in the palm (at the line drawn from the fully abducted thumb), the deep arch more proximally.

truncus-coeliacus.summary: The first anterior branch of the abdominal aorta; it supplies the foregut derivatives – stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, part of the pancreas and the upper half of the duodenum.
facts: Abdominal aorta (T12, just below the aortic hiatus)
Runs forward as a short trunk and soon divides into three branches
Left gastric artery, common hepatic artery (proper hepatic artery, gastroduodenal artery, right gastric artery), splenic artery
Abdominal oesophagus, stomach, upper duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen
clinical: A duodenal ulcer on the posterior wall can erode the gastroduodenal artery and cause severe bleeding.
Median arcuate ligament syndrome is external compression of the coeliac trunk.
tus: In median arcuate ligament syndrome the coeliac trunk is compressed by the crura of the diaphragm.
The pancreaticoduodenal arcades are an important collateral path between the coeliac and SMA systems.

a-mesenterica-superior.summary: Artery that supplies the midgut derivatives – from the lower half of the duodenum to two thirds of the transverse colon.
facts: Abdominal aorta (L1, 1 cm below the coeliac trunk)
Emerges behind the neck of the pancreas, passes in front of the left renal vein and the 3rd part of the duodenum and enters the mesentery
Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, jejunal and ileal arteries, ileocolic artery (appendicular artery), right colic artery, middle colic artery
Lower half of the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon, head of the pancreas
clinical: Acute mesenteric ischaemia (mostly embolic) presents with 'severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination'.
Nutcracker syndrome: compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and the SMA.
In SMA syndrome the 3rd part of the duodenum is compressed between the aorta and the artery.
tus: SMA embolism is the commonest cause of acute mesenteric ischaemia; 'severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination' is typical.
The neck of the pancreas and the splenic vein pass in front of the SMA; the left renal vein and the 3rd part of the duodenum pass behind it.

a-mesenterica-inferior.summary: Artery that supplies the hindgut derivatives – from the last third of the transverse colon to the upper rectum.
facts: Abdominal aorta (L3)
Descends retroperitoneally to the left
Left colic artery, sigmoid arteries, superior rectal (anorectal) artery
Distal 1/3 of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, upper rectum
sections: The marginal artery (of Drummond) joins the SMA and IMA branches along the edge of the colon. The splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) is the watershed between the two systems and therefore the site most vulnerable to ischaemia.
clinical: The IMA may be ligated in abdominal aortic aneurysm surgery, with a risk of colonic ischaemia.
tus: The IMA arises from the aorta at L3, about 3–4 cm above the bifurcation.
The IMA may be ligated during repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm; the colon is then supplied through the marginal artery.
